The Imperial Japanese Army. The military ground force of Imperial Japan, operating from the Meiji Restoration through World War II. It emerged as a conscript-based, Western-trained institution that uniquely blended European military science with samurai honor codes, emphasizing duty, loyalty, and honor unto death. The organization became increasingly politicized in the nineteen twenties and thirties, with radical factions plotting coups and pushing aggressive foreign policy. Military cliques gradually gained control over civilian government, marginalizing democratic institutions entirely. The army conquered vast territories across China and Manchuria, establishing the puppet state of Manchukuo and fighting the Second Sino-Japanese War from nineteen thirty-seven to nineteen forty-five, which killed an estimated twenty million Chinese civilians and soldiers. It became known for extreme brutality, including mass atrocities like the Nanjing Massacre in nineteen thirty-seven, where Japanese soldiers killed three hundred thousand Chinese civilians and prisoners in a matter of weeks, along with systematic torture, rape, and abuse of prisoners of war from multiple nations. In the Pacific, the army fought major campaigns at Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa, inflicting heavy casualties on Allied forces but suffering devastating defeats as American industrial capacity overwhelmed Japanese resources. The army organized suicide-attack units known as kamikaze, embodying the code that surrender was dishonorable and death was preferable. Over three thousand kamikaze pilots died in deliberate suicide attacks against Allied ships in the final year of the war. Approximately three million military deaths occurred during World War II, and Japanese and occupied territories' civilian casualties from combat, disease, starvation, and forced labor far exceeded military deaths, with historians estimating between ten and twenty million deaths across Asia.
